objectives: Trace the open + closed fuel cycle.

slides.title: The nuclear fuel cycle: open vs closed
slides.body:
**Open (once-through) fuel cycle** — current US + most countries:

1. **Mining**: open-pit or underground; in-situ leaching. Top producers: Kazakhstan (45%), Canada (15%), Australia (12%), Namibia, Niger.
2. **Milling**: U₃O₈ (yellowcake) ~85% pure U.
3. **Conversion**: yellowcake → UF₆ gas.
4. **Enrichment**: separation of U-235 from U-238 via centrifuge (modern) or gaseous diffusion (legacy). Output: low-enriched UF₆ (3-5% U-235) + depleted UF₆ tails (0.2-0.3%).
5. **Fuel fabrication**: UF₆ → UO₂ → pellets → fuel rods → assemblies.
6. **Reactor**: 18-24 months residence; ~50 GWd/t burnup.
7. **Spent fuel pool**: 5-10 yr cooling in water on-site.
8. **Dry cask storage**: on-site after pool cooling; ~50 yr design life. Most US spent fuel here now (~85,000 tonnes accumulated).
9. **Geological repository**: planned long-term disposal — none operating commercially yet for high-level waste.

**Closed (reprocessing) fuel cycle** — France, Russia, Japan (Rokkasho), formerly UK:

After step 7 (pool cooling): chemical reprocessing extracts U + Pu, fabricates MOX (mixed oxide fuel: ~7% Pu + 93% U), re-uses in reactors. Reduces high-level waste volume + recovers ~25% more energy. France runs ~70% MOX in ~20 of its reactors.

**Trade-offs**:
- Closed cycle: better fuel utilization; less waste volume; but proliferation risk (separated Pu); higher cost ($5000-10000/kg fuel vs $2000-3000 open); requires specialized facilities.
- Open cycle: cheaper; simpler; but accumulates spent fuel; loses Pu energy.

slides.title: Enrichment + separation work
slides.body:
**Enrichment** is the energy-intensive step. SI unit: **Separative Work Unit (SWU)** — measure of enrichment effort.

For 1 kg of 3.5% U-235 product from 0.72% natural with 0.2% tails:
- Feed: 5.45 kg natural U
- Tails: 4.45 kg at 0.2%
- Work: ~4.5 SWU/kg product

Global enrichment capacity: ~64 million SWU/yr (2024). Russia: ~40% market share. China + Western Europe + US: rest. Costs: ~$50-80/SWU.

**Centrifuge technology**: gas of UF₆ spun at ~70,000 rpm; isotope separation via tiny mass difference (U-235 vs U-238 = 0.86% mass difference). Many cascaded centrifuges → ~5-6 SWU per kg of U separated. Modern Western cascade: ~10× more efficient than 1950s gaseous diffusion.

**Weapons-grade**: ~90% U-235. Requires ~200-300 SWU per kg (~50× more work than 3.5% LEU). High-enriched uranium (HEU) is the canonical proliferation concern.

**HALEU** (High-Assay LEU, 5-20%): for advanced reactors (some SMRs, MSR, fast reactors). Russia currently dominates supply; US + EU developing domestic enrichment (Centrus, Urenco) for SMR fleet.

**Laser enrichment** (e.g., GE-Hitachi SILEX): potentially more efficient + smaller-footprint. Licensed in US (Paducah enrichment site Nov 2023, but commercial scaling slow).

**Other separation methods**:
- Gaseous diffusion (legacy, energy-intensive, decommissioned)
- Aerodynamic (South Africa nozzle, decommissioned)
- Calutron (Manhattan Project; uneconomic at scale)
- Plasma separation (research)
- Chemical exchange (heavy water D₂O production)

slides.title: Geological disposal + the long-term challenge
slides.body:
Spent fuel after ~50 yr cooling still contains:
• ~96% U (mostly U-238 + 1-2% U-235)
• ~1-2% Pu + Np + Am (transuranic actinides) — long-lived
• ~3-4% fission products (Cs-137, Sr-90, I-129, Tc-99, etc.)

Radioactivity drops ~10⁵× in first 100 yr (short-lived fission products decay). After 1000 yr, fission products mostly decayed. Remaining hazard from actinides (Pu-239 t½ = 24000 yr; Np-237 t½ = 2.1 million yr).

**Total hazard** (radiotoxicity-weighted) decays to natural-uranium-ore equivalent after ~250,000 yr (open cycle) or ~10,000 yr (closed cycle with actinide partition + transmutation).

**Geological repository requirements**:
• Stable geology for 100,000+ yr (no earthquakes, no glaciation through host rock).
• Low groundwater flow (to limit transport of radionuclides).
• Engineered barriers (copper canister, bentonite buffer, host rock).
• Multi-barrier defense in depth.

**Operating + active repositories** (2024):
• **Olkiluoto, Finland (Onkalo)**: first operational deep geological repository (DGR) for spent fuel, expected first emplacement 2025. ~400 m depth in granite. Copper canister + bentonite + crystalline rock.
• **Forsmark, Sweden**: license granted 2022; construction starting; analogous to Finnish design.
• **France (Cigéo, Bure)**: in advanced authorization phase. Argilite clay host.
• **Switzerland (Bois de Boën / Nördlich Lägern)**: opalinus clay; construction ~2050.
• **Belgium (Dessel)**: clay; in early development.
• **US (Yucca Mountain)**: licensed but politically blocked; alternative siting under consideration.
• **WIPP, New Mexico**: operational since 1999 for transuranic waste only (defense-program); deep salt repository.

**Public + political challenges**:
- 'Not in my backyard' (NIMBY): no community wants to host
- Trust + transparency: requires long-term institutional commitment
- Indigenous + heritage land considerations
- Cost: $10-50B per repository; financed via spent-fuel surcharges on electricity

**Alternatives + future**:
- Actinide partition + transmutation (P&T): chemically separate long-lived actinides + transmute in fast reactors → reduces waste timescale to ~1000 yr. Active research at JAEA (Japan), ANL, INL (US), CEA (France).
- Deep borehole disposal (5+ km drilling): emerging concept; isolated from biosphere via huge depth + sediment.
- Spent-fuel reuse in advanced reactors (e.g., TerraPower TWR concept).

Geological disposal works (physics + geology) but is hard (politics + economics + time). Finnish achievement gives playbook for others.

question.question: Track Pu-239 from U-238 in an LWR + closed fuel cycle
question.goal: U-238 (0.72% U-235 in natural U; ~95.5% U-238 in 3.5% LEU after enrichment) captures neutrons in reactor + becomes Pu-239 via β decay. Trace the chemistry + economic value.

steps.reveal: U-238 + n → U-239 (t½=23 min, β⁻) → Np-239 (t½=2.4 d, β⁻) → Pu-239 (t½=24,000 yr, α). All three steps fast enough that within ~3 d, captured U-238 becomes Pu-239.

steps.prompt: Pu-239 in spent fuel: ~1 wt% of original heavy metal. For a 1000 MWe reactor with ~20 t spent fuel/yr, how much Pu?
steps.reveal: ~200 kg Pu/yr per 1000 MWe reactor (open cycle, not reprocessed). World accumulation: ~70,000 t spent fuel × 1% Pu ≈ 700 tonnes Pu in spent fuel globally.

steps.prompt: If recovered as MOX (~7% Pu in fuel), how much MOX can be made?
steps.reveal: ~2900 kg MOX fuel/yr (mass dilution with U). MOX fuel can substitute for fresh enriched fuel in MOX-licensed reactors. France runs ~20 reactors on MOX.

steps.prompt: Energy recovered from MOX vs original fresh LEU?
hints: Recovered U + Pu can substitute ~25-30% of fresh fuel.
steps.reveal: Reprocessing + MOX recovers ~25-30% additional energy from spent fuel — modest improvement. The biggest win would be Pu (fast spectrum) breeders: ~50-100× more energy per kg natural U. But breeder economics haven't worked yet at commercial scale (sodium-cooled fast reactor costs higher than LWR; uranium remains abundant).

hints: Pu-239 is fissile + makes weapons feasible.
steps.reveal: Separated Pu (reprocessed but not yet in MOX fuel) is the primary proliferation concern. ~7 kg of weapons-grade Pu (>93% Pu-239) sufficient for a primitive weapon. Reactor-grade Pu (60-70% Pu-239, rest Pu-240, 241, 242 + Am-241) is harder + less reliable for weapons but technically usable. Hence IAEA safeguards on reprocessing facilities + Pu inventory tracking. NPT-signatory states with reprocessing (UK shut down 2018, France, Russia, Japan, India) accept IAEA inspection. Non-NPT or non-cooperative states cause proliferation concerns (e.g., North Korea).

question.question: Why has the US not built a geological repository despite spending billions on Yucca Mountain?
options: Technical + political stalemate. Technically: NRC + DOE characterized Yucca extensively; license application submitted 2008; final design phase. Politically: Nevada delegation (Senate majority leader Reid) blocked funding from 2009-onwards; Obama administration suspended program; license application withdrawn 2010. Successor administrations have not committed to either restart or alternative siting. Result: ~85,000 tonnes spent fuel + defense HLW stored on-site at reactor sites + DOE facilities. Multiple states (TX, NM) recently proposed alternatives (Holtec interim storage) — also legally contested.
All US spent fuel is in space.
question.explanation:
**Yucca Mountain history**:

- 1982: Nuclear Waste Policy Act — DOE responsibility, ratepayers fund via Nuclear Waste Fund.
- 1987: Yucca Mountain (Nevada, Nye County) chosen by Congress.
- 1990s-2000s: $14B+ characterization. Geological + hydrological studies + engineered barriers + transportation network planning.
- 2002: Bush administration formally designated YM as repository.
- 2008: DOE submitted license application to NRC.
- 2010: Obama administration withdrew license application + suspended program (Nevada delegation political pressure).
- 2011: Blue Ribbon Commission recommended *consent-based* siting (Nevada had not consented).
- 2017: Trump administration proposed reviving; not funded.
- 2020s: stalemate. Some technical experts argue Yucca is sound; others want alternatives.

**Consequence**:
- ~85,000 t spent fuel in dry casks + pools at ~75 reactor sites.
- DOE liable for breach of contract (originally promised to take fuel from 1998); paying $5-10B in damages to utilities.
- Spent fuel inventory growing ~2000 t/yr.
- Interim storage facilities (Holtec NM, ISP/Waste Control Specialists TX) licensed but legally challenged.

**Alternatives being explored**:
- Consent-based siting (DOE process started 2022 after Biden administration).
- Interim consolidated storage (decades) + later geological disposal.
- Defense waste + civilian waste in same facility (legally complex).
- Deep borehole disposal (5+ km drilling).

**International contrast**:
- Finland: site selected 1983, construction 2004, operation 2025 (~40 yr cycle).
- Sweden: license 2022, construction underway.
- France: Cigéo authorization 2030, operation ~2035-2040.

Difference: Finland + Sweden used **consent-based siting** + sustained political support across decades. The US Yucca process violated consent (Nevada didn't agree); has been politically contested ever since.

**Cost of delay**: $5-10B/decade in damages + ongoing storage costs + missed reprocessing optionality.

**Lesson**: technical solvability ≠ political deliverability. Long-term radioactive waste disposal requires multi-decade institutional commitment + community consent.

slides.workedSolution: Yucca Mountain technically characterized + license app submitted 2008. Politically blocked by Nevada delegation; license app withdrawn 2010; never operational. Result: ~85K t spent fuel at reactor sites + DOE liability ($5-10B in damages, growing). Alternative: consent-based siting process (re-started 2022). International contrast: Finland/Sweden used consent-based siting + sustained political will → operating 2025. US lesson: technical solvability ≠ political deliverability.

question.question: Why has fast-reactor + reprocessing-based closed fuel cycle not displaced once-through LWR despite ~50× theoretical fuel-utilization advantage?
options: Economics: uranium has been abundant + cheap (<$50/lb U₃O₈), reprocessing costs ~5-10× more per kg fuel than fresh LEU; fast reactor capital cost ~2× LWR; combined economics unfavorable at low U price. Proliferation: separated Pu inventory + reprocessing facilities are sensitive — Western non-proliferation policy historically resisted. France + Russia + Japan continued; UK + US gave up. Modern revival: countries seeking fuel-cycle independence + waste reduction (China, India, Russia) actively pursuing; commercial competitive 2030-2050 horizon depending on U price + carbon constraints.
question.explanation:
**Closed fuel cycle economics + politics history**:

- 1950s-60s: closed cycle assumed inevitable. Fast breeders projected to dominate.
- 1970s: US Carter administration banned commercial reprocessing (1977) over proliferation concerns. Spent fuel pile-up began.
- 1980s-90s: France (La Hague), UK (Sellafield), Russia (Mayak) operated. Uranium remained cheap.
- 2000s: UK Sellafield reprocessing accidents → closed 2018. France continues. Russia ramping. Japan Rokkasho delayed repeatedly.
- 2010s-now: Renewed interest from China + India (fuel-cycle independence) + Russia (BN-800 operational); some Western interest (TerraPower Natrium, MOX) for waste reduction + advanced reactor fuel.

**Economics gap**:
- Once-through LEU: ~$2000-3000/kg fuel, $1000-2000 in fuel cost per MWh generated.
- MOX (closed cycle): ~$10,000-20,000/kg fuel, $3000-5000 per MWh.
- Difference partly subsidies (reprocessing in France benefits from sunk costs); partly intrinsic.

**Why uranium stays cheap**: discovered reserves are huge; new exploration adds reserves faster than depletion. Estimated U reserves at $130/kg: ~7.6 million tonnes — ~140 years of current LWR consumption. At $260/kg: ~16 million tonnes (~290 years). Beyond conventional: phosphate rock + seawater (~4.5 billion t but expensive). Uranium is *not* the bottleneck for nuclear scale-up.

**Proliferation concern**: separated Pu inventory ~ 250 tonnes globally (France 110t + UK 140t + Japan 8t + Russia 60t). Pu is fissile; 6-8 kg sufficient for primitive weapon. IAEA safeguards + national security oversight required. Some weapons-state Pu (e.g., post-Cold-War US + Russia surplus) is being diluted + burned in MOX reactors specifically to reduce stockpiles.

**Closed cycle would matter if**:
- U price spikes due to ramped LWR fleet + China + India growth (possible 2030-2050)
- Carbon pricing makes once-through LWR less competitive
- Waste-disposal politics force reprocessing to reduce volume
- Advanced reactors (fast spectrum) deploy at scale + need recycled fuel

**Long-term**: closed cycle + actinide partition + transmutation is the only physics-based path to 'sustainable' nuclear with minimized long-lived waste. Whether economics align with this physics over 21st century is the open question.

hints: What's been the U price history?
slides.workedSolution: Closed cycle economics: U cheap (<$50/lb), reprocessing 5-10× more than fresh LEU, fast reactor capital ~2× LWR. Proliferation: separated Pu sensitive; US banned commercial reprocessing 1977; France/Russia/Japan continued. Renewed interest: China + India (fuel independence), TerraPower Natrium (waste). Closed cycle competitive if U spikes (LWR fleet growth) or carbon pricing tightens or waste politics force volume reduction. Long-term sustainable nuclear physics requires closed cycle + actinide P&T.

question.question: Spent fuel has 3 wt% fission products + 1 wt% transuranic + 96 wt% U. If a 1000 MWe reactor produces 20 tonnes spent fuel/yr, how much fission product (in kg) accumulates per year?

question.prompt: In ≤120 words, explain to a curious citizen why nuclear waste disposal is technically solvable but politically + temporally challenging.
question.rubric: Mentions: technically — deep geological repositories in stable formations (granite, clay, salt) provide multi-barrier defense (engineered canister + bentonite + host rock). Time scales (100K+ yr) match natural geological stability. Finland, Sweden, France, Switzerland have technical paths + repositories planned or operating. Politically — long timescales beyond political cycles; no community wants to host (NIMBY); requires consent-based siting + transparent institutional commitment across decades; trust-building with Indigenous + heritage communities. Temporally — institutional permanence required (records, markers, monitoring) for thousands of years; intergenerational equity questions. Economic — $10-50B per repository; financing via ratepayer surcharges; uncertainty about future fuel-cycle decisions. Best practices: Finnish + Swedish consent-based siting works; US Yucca-style imposition does not. Future technologies (actinide P&T, deep borehole) may reduce timescale + simplify problem. Concludes: solvable problem requiring institutional discipline + community engagement, not technological breakthrough.
